The Verification Tax: Fundamental Limits of AI Auditing
in the Rare-Error Regime

Jason Z Wang Affiliation: Independent Email: jasonhearlte@gmail.com
Abstract

The most cited calibration result in deep learning—post-temperature-scaling ECE of 0.012 on CIFAR-100 (Guo et al., 2017)—is below the statistical noise floor. We prove this is not a failure of the experiment but a law: the minimax rate for estimating calibration error with model error rate ε\varepsilon is Θ⁡((L​ε/m)1/3)\Theta((L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}), and no estimator can beat it. This “verification tax” implies that as AI models improve, verifying their calibration becomes fundamentally harder—with the same exponent in opposite directions. We establish four results that contradict standard evaluation practice: (1) self-evaluation without labels provides exactly zero information about calibration, bounded by a constant independent of compute; (2) a sharp phase transition at m⋅ε≈1m\cdot\varepsilon\approx 1 below which miscalibration is undetectable; (3) active querying eliminates the Lipschitz constant, collapsing estimation to detection; (4) verification cost grows exponentially with pipeline depth at rate LKL^{K}. We validate across five benchmarks (MMLU, TruthfulQA, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande; ∼27,000{\sim}27{,}000 items) with 6 LLMs from 5 families (8B–405B parameters, 27 benchmark–model pairs with logprob-based confidence), 95% bootstrap CIs, and permutation tests. Self-evaluation non-significance holds in 80% of pairs. Across frontier models, 23% of pairwise comparisons are indistinguishable from noise, implying that credible calibration claims must report verification floors and prioritize active querying once gains approach benchmark resolution.

1 Introduction

The base rate problem—that rare conditions are hard to detect—is among the oldest results in statistics. We show that AI auditing faces the same fundamental barrier. The “disease” is miscalibration: the gap between a model’s stated confidence and its actual accuracy. As errors become rare, miscalibration becomes a rare condition, and the verification cost grows without bound. We call this the verification tax. In one line: better models are harder to audit.

This result completes a programme initiated by Sun et al. (2023), who established the O(n−2/3)O(n^{-2/3}) upper bound for ECE estimation (NeurIPS 2023 Spotlight), and extended by Futami and Fujisawa (2024), who generalized the rate information-theoretically (NeurIPS 2024). Both left two questions open: (1) Is n−1/3n^{-1/3} the optimal rate? (2) How does the model’s error rate ε\varepsilon affect verification difficulty? We resolve both. The lower bound (Theorem 2) matches the upper bound (Theorem 3), establishing (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3} as the minimax rate. The ε\varepsilon-dependence—absent from all prior work—reveals a phase transition, a scaling duality, and a verification horizon.

The tax is a law: no estimator can beat Θ⁡((L​ε/m)1/3)\Theta((L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}). Under meaningful verification (δ=Θ⁡(ε)\delta=\Theta(\varepsilon)), sample complexity grows as Ω⁡(1/ε2)\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{2}). Capability and verifiability are governed by the same exponent in opposite directions (Theorem 4).

But the rate is the scaffolding. The paper’s contributions are four results that contradict standard assumptions in AI evaluation (Liang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024):

Surprise 1: Self-evaluation is bounded by a constant (§3). Any estimator that does not use ground-truth labels—including LLM-as-Judge, self-consistency, chain-of-thought verification, and all model-derived signals—has worst-case calibration error ≥1/2\geq 1/2 for L≥1L\geq 1. The bound is independent of the number of queries. White-box model access does not help unless it identifies a low-dimensional parametric family.

Surprise 2: There is a sharp phase transition (§4). Below m⋅ε≈1m\cdot\varepsilon\approx 1, miscalibration is undetectable by any method. We show that most published safety benchmark improvements fall below the verification floor (Table 1), and 65% of MMLU per-subject rankings are noise.

Surprise 3: Active querying eliminates LL (§5). When the auditor chooses which inputs to test, the minimax rate improves to Θ⁡(ε/m)\Theta(\sqrt{\varepsilon/m})—the Lipschitz constant disappears entirely. We validate this on production LLMs: all three models collapse to the same active rate despite L^∈[1.4,2.5]\hat{L}\in[1.4,2.5].

Surprise 4: Composition is exponential (§6). A KK-component AI pipeline has verification cost Ω⁡(LK⋅ε/δ3)\Omega(L^{K}\cdot\varepsilon/\delta^{3}). A 10-step agent loop with L=2L=2 costs 1,024×1{,}024\times a single-step model. This applies to chain-of-thought, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic systems.

Together, these results imply that the dominant practices in AI evaluation—passive benchmarking, self-evaluation, and end-to-end testing of complex pipelines—operate in provably information-less regimes. We demonstrate this empirically and show that every frontier model exceeds the verification horizon (§7).

Concrete scale.

The law already bites on today’s benchmarks. On MMLU (n=14,042n{=}14{,}042, ε≈0.16\varepsilon{\approx}0.16, L^≈1.4\hat{L}{\approx}1.4), the calibration floor is about 0.0280.028, while the corresponding accuracy floor is only 0.0060.006: calibration is about 4.7×4.7\times harder to verify than accuracy. On TruthfulQA (n=817n{=}817), the floor rises to 0.0930.093–0.1390.139, large enough to swamp many reported improvements. Even if frontier models reach ε≈0.05\varepsilon\approx 0.05 on MMLU, the passive floor remains ≈0.016\approx 0.016–0.0180.018. The practical implication is simple: below-floor gains should be treated as ties unless the evaluator uses much larger holdouts or active querying.

2 The Verification Tax

Setup. Let ff be a classifier with confidence p⁡(x)∈[0,1]p(x)\in[0,1]. The calibration gap is Δ⁡(p)=η⁡(p)−p\Delta(p)=\eta(p)-p where η⁡(p)=𝔼⁡[Y=y^∣p⁡(X)=p]\eta(p)=\mathbb{E}[Y{=}\hat{y}\mid p(X){=}p]. The binned ECE is ECEB=∑b(nb/n)​|Δ¯b|\mathrm{ECE}_{B}=\sum_{b}(n_{b}/n)|\bar{\Delta}_{b}|. We consider LL-Lipschitz calibration functions ℱ⁡(L)={Δ:|Δ⁡(p1)−Δ⁡(p2)|≤L​|p1−p2|}\mathcal{F}(L)=\{\Delta:|\Delta(p_{1})-\Delta(p_{2})|\leq L|p_{1}-p_{2}|\} and the minimax risk R∗​(m,ε,L)=infECE^supΔ∈ℱ⁡(L)𝔼⁡[|ECE^−ECE|]R^{*}(m,\varepsilon,L)=\inf_{\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}}\sup_{\Delta\in\mathcal{F}(L)}\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}-\mathrm{ECE}|], where ε=Pr[Y≠y^]\varepsilon=\Pr[Y\neq\hat{y}] is the error rate.

Theorem 1 (Le Cam Lower Bound).

R∗​(m,ε,L)≥c1​ε/mR^{*}(m,\varepsilon,L)\geq c_{1}\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}, where c1≥1/(4​2)c_{1}\geq 1/(4\sqrt{2}).

Proof sketch.

Construct P0P_{0} (calibrated, ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0) and P1P_{1} (miscalibrated by δ\delta) at p0=1−εp_{0}=1-\varepsilon. KL divergence: m​δ2/εm\delta^{2}/\varepsilon. Setting KL=1\mathrm{KL}=1 via Bretagnolle–Huber gives R∗≥(1/2​e)​ε/mR^{*}\geq(1/2e)\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}. Full proof: Appendix H. ∎

Theorem 2 (Minimax Lower Bound).

Under score-mass concentration near 1−ε1{-}\varepsilon, R∗​(m,ε,L)≥c2​(L​ε/m)1/3⋅(log⁡m)−c3R^{*}(m,\varepsilon,L)\geq c_{2}(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}\cdot(\log m)^{-c_{3}}.

Proof sketch.

The full proof (Appendix B) constructs two product priors on LL-Lipschitz calibration functions directly in the Bernoulli observation model, following the two-prior method of Lepski et al. (1999). The construction uses a signed measure that separates L1L_{1} norms while controlling the Bernoulli KL divergence, yielding the rate (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3} up to logarithmic factors without invoking asymptotic equivalence to white noise. An alternative derivation via Brown–Low equivalence (Brown and Low, 1996) is in Appendix K. ∎

Theorem 3 (Matched Upper Bound).

Histogram binning with B∗=⌊(L2​m/ε)1/3⌋B^{*}=\lfloor(L^{2}m/\varepsilon)^{1/3}\rfloor achieves 𝔼⁡[|ECE^B∗−ECE|]≤C​(L​ε/m)1/3\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}_{B^{*}}-\mathrm{ECE}|]\leq C(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}.

Proof sketch.

Bias ≤L/B\leq L/B, variance ≤ε​B/m\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon B/m}. Optimize at B∗=(L2​m/ε)1/3B^{*}=(L^{2}m/\varepsilon)^{1/3}. ∎

The polynomial rate (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3} is established by matching upper and lower bounds. The lower bound carries a logarithmic correction (log⁡m)−c′(\log m)^{-c^{\prime}} inherited from the structure of L1L_{1} functional estimation: the non-smoothness of |t||t| at zero requires a Fourier-analytic construction whose truncation introduces the logarithmic loss. This is the same gap identified by Lepski et al. (1999) twenty-seven years ago, and it remains open whether the gap belongs in the lower bound or the upper bound. We conjecture that the minimax rate is exactly Θ⁡((L​ε/m)1/3)\Theta((L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}) with no logarithmic correction. Resolving this would settle a longstanding question in nonparametric functional estimation, independent of the AI auditing application.

Theorem 4 (Scaling Duality).

If ε⁡(N)=c0​N−α\varepsilon(N)=c_{0}N^{-\alpha} for α>0\alpha>0, then under meaningful verification (δ=Θ⁡(ε)\delta=\Theta(\varepsilon)), the sample complexity satisfies m⁡(N)=Ω⁡(Nα)m(N)=\Omega(N^{\alpha}). Capability and verifiability scale with the same exponent in opposite directions.

Corollary 5 (Phase Transition).

Taking δ=ε\delta=\varepsilon: detection is impossible for m<c12/εm<c_{1}^{2}/\varepsilon and possible for m>C/εm>C/\varepsilon. The transition occurs at m∗≍1/εm^{*}\asymp 1/\varepsilon.

Corollary 6 (Benchmark Resolution Limit).

For a benchmark of nn items, the minimum detectable calibration difference between two models is δmin=(L​ε/n)1/3\delta_{\min}=(L\varepsilon/n)^{1/3}. Rankings of models whose differences fall within δmin\delta_{\min} are statistically indistinguishable from noise.

3 Surprise 1: Self-Evaluation Provides Zero Information

Theorem 7 (Self-Verification Impossibility).

Let z⁡(x)=g⁡(x,θ)z(x)=g(x,\theta) be any auxiliary signal derived from the model. Any estimator V⁡(x1,p1,z1,…,xm,pm,zm)V(x_{1},p_{1},z_{1},\ldots,x_{m},p_{m},z_{m}) that does not use true labels satisfies: supΔ∈ℱ⁡(L)𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δ)|]≥min⁡(L,1)/2\sup_{\Delta\in\mathcal{F}(L)}\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta)|]\geq\min(L,1)/2.

Proof.

Δ0≡0\Delta_{0}\equiv 0 and Δ1≡min⁡(L,1)\Delta_{1}\equiv\min(L,1) produce identical observations (xi,pi,zi)(x_{i},p_{i},z_{i}) for any model. Any label-free estimator returns the same value under both, so it errs by ≥min⁡(L,1)/2\geq\min(L,1)/2 on at least one. ∎

Corollary 8 (LLM-as-Judge Impossibility).

Let JJ be any evaluator model. If JJ’s evaluation of subject model SS relies solely on (xi,fS​(xi))(x_{i},f_{S}(x_{i}))—inputs and outputs, without ground-truth labels—then supΔ𝔼⁡[|VJ−ECE|]≥1/2\sup_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}[|V_{J}-\mathrm{ECE}|]\geq 1/2 for L≥1L\geq 1, regardless of JJ’s capability or the number of evaluations. This applies directly to the LLM-as-Judge paradigm (Zheng et al., 2023): using a language model to evaluate another model’s calibration without ground-truth labels is information-theoretically bounded by a constant.

Corollary 9 (Hallucination Detection Wall).

Factual accuracy is a special case of calibration. Self-consistency methods (sampling multiple responses, checking agreement) operate without labels and incur worst-case error ≥1/2\geq 1/2. Self-reported hallucination rates have zero information-theoretic content.

Corollary 10 (Instance-Dependent Self-Verification Impossibility).

For any label-free estimator VV and any δ∈(0,min⁡(L,1)]\delta\in(0,\min(L,1)]: supΔ∈ℱ⁡(L),ECE⁡(Δ)=δ𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δ)|]≥δ/2\sup_{\Delta\in\mathcal{F}(L),\,\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta)=\delta}\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta)|]\geq\delta/2. That is, for every ECE value δ\delta, there exists a calibration function with that ECE that any label-free estimator will mis-estimate by at least δ/2\delta/2.

Proof.

Fix δ\delta. Let Δ0≡0\Delta_{0}\equiv 0 (ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0) and Δδ\Delta_{\delta} with ECE=δ\mathrm{ECE}=\delta. Both produce identical label-free observations. For any VV: 𝔼⁡[|V−0|]+𝔼⁡[|V−δ|]≥δ\mathbb{E}[|V-0|]+\mathbb{E}[|V-\delta|]\geq\delta. Thus max⁡{𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δ0)|],𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δδ)|]}≥δ/2\max\{\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{0})|],\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{\delta})|]\}\geq\delta/2. ∎

Theorem 11 (White-Box Irrelevance).

Let 𝒮=σ⁡(θ,A,Dtrain)\mathcal{S}=\sigma(\theta,A,D_{\mathrm{train}}). Any 𝒮\mathcal{S}-measurable estimator using mm fresh samples satisfies R𝒮∗≥c​ε/mR^{*}_{\mathcal{S}}\geq c\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}. White-box access helps only by constraining Δ\Delta to a parametric family (Corollary: dd-dimensional family ⇒\Rightarrow O⁡(1/m)O(1/\sqrt{m}) rate).

Empirical validation. Figure 1 confirms the theory on MMLU (14,042 items, 3 models). Left: confidence predicts accuracy (Spearman ρ=0.55\rho=0.55–0.950.95, all p<0.05p<0.05). Right: confidence does not predict calibration gap magnitude (ρ=0.39\rho=0.39–0.530.53, 2/3 non-significant). Self-confidence tells you whether you are right, not how wrong your confidence is.

4 Surprise 2: Phase Transition and the Demolition

The phase transition (Corollary 5) predicts a sharp wall at m⋅ε≈1m\cdot\varepsilon\approx 1. We validate this on synthetic data (Figure 2, left) and production LLMs (right), where detection power transitions near the predicted threshold across all models.

The benchmark demolition. Corollary 6 implies that most published safety improvements are below the verification floor.

Of 11 major benchmarks, 7 have typical claimed improvements below the verification floor (L=1L{=}1). Zero are robustly verifiable. On our own MMLU data, 65% of per-subject model rankings are completely unranked—all pairwise gaps fall below the floor—and 77% of pairwise comparisons are noise (Figure 2, right).

Are the differences between frontier models real? We compute pairwise accuracy gaps between published scores for GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini Ultra, and Llama-3-405B across four benchmarks. Of 64 pairwise comparisons, 23% are unverifiable or marginal (Table 2). On GPQA Diamond (n=198n{=}198), zero of three model pairs are statistically distinguishable. On HumanEval (n=164n{=}164), 40% of pairs are unverifiable or marginal. Even on MMLU (n=14,042n{=}14{,}042), GPT-4 vs. Claude 3 Opus (gap 0.4%, floor 0.6%) is noise. The top of the leaderboard is, in substantial part, a tie.

5 Surprise 3: Active Querying Eliminates LL

Theorem 12 (Active Verification Rate).

With adaptive confidence-level selection, Ractive∗​(m,ε,L)=Θ⁡(ε/m)R^{*}_{\mathrm{active}}(m,\varepsilon,L)=\Theta(\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}). The Lipschitz constant disappears entirely.

Proof sketch.

Lower: Chain rule of KL; per-observation information is δ2/ε\delta^{2}/\varepsilon regardless of adaptivity. Upper: Two-phase explore-exploit. Phase 1: resolve sign of Δ\Delta on NN grid points. Phase 2: estimate |Δ||\Delta| in resolved bins. Set N=L​m/εN=L\sqrt{m/\varepsilon}; both terms become O⁡(ε/m)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}). Full proof: Appendix C. ∎

The gap between passive ((L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}) and active (ε/m\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}) is (L2​m/ε)1/6(L^{2}m/\varepsilon)^{1/6}. For L=2.5L=2.5, m=10,000m=10{,}000, ε=0.16\varepsilon=0.16: active is ∼\sim5×\times more efficient.

Empirical validation on MMLU. Figure 3 validates Theorem 12 on production data. Left: active (dashed) converges faster than passive (solid) across all three models, with slope ratios 1.38–1.48 (theory: 1.50). Right: at fixed m=2000m{=}2000, active errors are {0.0091,0.0092,0.0077}\{0.0091,0.0092,0.0077\} across models with L^∈{1.41,2.01,2.45}\hat{L}\in\{1.41,2.01,2.45\} (coefficient of variation 8%)—confirming LL-independence.

6 Surprise 4: Composition Is Exponential

Theorem 13 (Compositional Verification Tax).

For a KK-component pipeline with per-component Lipschitz L1,…,LKL_{1},\ldots,L_{K}: Lsys≤∏kLk+1L_{\mathrm{sys}}\leq\prod_{k}L_{k}+1, and msys=Ω⁡(Lsys⋅ε/δ3)m_{\mathrm{sys}}=\Omega(L_{\mathrm{sys}}\cdot\varepsilon/\delta^{3}). For homogeneous Lk=L>1L_{k}=L>1: msys=Ω⁡(LK⋅ε/δ3)m_{\mathrm{sys}}=\Omega(L^{K}\cdot\varepsilon/\delta^{3})—exponential in pipeline depth.

Maximum verifiable depth: Kmax=⌊logL⁡(Mtotal​δ3/ε)⌋K_{\mathrm{max}}=\lfloor\log_{L}(M_{\mathrm{total}}\delta^{3}/\varepsilon)\rfloor. An agent with 10 reasoning steps at L=2L{=}2: 1,024×1{,}024\times cost. At L=2L{=}2, K=20K{=}20: over 106×10^{6}\times. The Lipschitz composition model applies to continuous reasoning chains (chain-of-thought, iterative refinement). Discontinuous components such as retrieval or tool use have Lk=∞L_{k}=\infty, making end-to-end verification infeasible at any sample size for such pipelines.

Theorem 14 (General Verification Tax).

For any verification functional V⁡(Δ,μG)=∫|Δ⁡(p)|​d​μG​(p)V(\Delta,\mu_{G})=\int|\Delta(p)|\,d\mu_{G}(p) with LL-Lipschitz integrand, effective noise σ2\sigma^{2}, and effective sample meffm_{\mathrm{eff}}: passive rate Θ⁡((L​σ2/meff)1/3)\Theta((L\sigma^{2}/m_{\mathrm{eff}})^{1/3}); active rate Θ⁡(σ2/meff)\Theta(\sqrt{\sigma^{2}/m_{\mathrm{eff}}}). Instantiations: calibration (GG = population), fairness (meff=m​πm_{\mathrm{eff}}=m\pi), robustness (σ2=εpert\sigma^{2}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pert}}).

Corollary 15 (Fairness Tax).

For a group with proportion π\pi, verification requires m≥(1/π)⋅L​ε/δ3m\geq(1/\pi)\cdot L\varepsilon/\delta^{3}. A 5% minority group costs 20×20\times the full population.

7 The Verification Horizon

Theorem 16 (Verification Horizon).

Let ε⁡(N)=c0​N−α\varepsilon(N)=c_{0}N^{-\alpha} and MtotalM_{\mathrm{total}} be total labeled data. The verification floor is δfloor​(N)=(L​ε​(N)/Mtotal)1/3\delta_{\mathrm{floor}}(N)=(L\varepsilon(N)/M_{\mathrm{total}})^{1/3}. Meaningful verification requires N<N∗=(c02​Mtotal/L)1/(2​α)N<N^{*}=(c_{0}^{2}M_{\mathrm{total}}/L)^{1/(2\alpha)}.

Under Chinchilla scaling (α≈0.5\alpha\approx 0.5, c0≈1c_{0}\approx 1, L=1L=1, Mtotal=14,000M_{\mathrm{total}}=14{,}000): N∗≈107N^{*}\approx 10^{7}—well below current frontier models (>1011>10^{11}). Across the domains we audit, every frontier system exceeds the passive horizon by orders of magnitude; representative calculations are deferred to Appendix G. Active verification shifts the horizon to Nactive∗=(c0​Mtotal)1/αN^{*}_{\mathrm{active}}=(c_{0}M_{\mathrm{total}})^{1/\alpha}, but no current evaluation framework supports active querying at scale.

Regulatory infeasibility.

The fairness tax (Corollary 15) compounds with the base verification tax across demographic subgroups. If evaluation must certify calibration to precision δ\delta across KK groups with minimum proportion πmin\pi_{\min}, then m≥K​L​ε/(πmin​δ3)m\geq KL\varepsilon/(\pi_{\min}\delta^{3}). Under illustrative EU AI Act Annex III settings (K=10K{=}10, πmin=0.05\pi_{\min}{=}0.05, δ=0.02\delta{=}0.02, ε=0.05\varepsilon{=}0.05), this requires 1.251.25M labels against ∼700{\sim}700K available medical-imaging labels. Appendix G reports the broader cross-framework comparison and assumptions.

Verification half-life.

Under ECE drift rate λ\lambda, every verification expires after t1/2=δ/λt_{1/2}=\delta/\lambda. Representative domains range from months (medical AI) to hours (financial trading), so even successful audits must be periodically renewed.

8 Empirical Validation

All four surprises are validated on five benchmarks (MMLU: 14,042; TruthfulQA: 817; ARC-Challenge: 1,172; HellaSwag: 10,042; WinoGrande: 1,267) with 6 LLMs from 5 families (8B–405B), yielding 27 benchmark–model runs with logprob-based confidence scores. All quantities carry 95% bootstrap CIs (1,000 replicates; Appendix S). Figure 5 shows how the ε\varepsilon-dependent rate diverges from prior work as models improve.

Results. (1) Self-confidence is uninformative about calibration gap: across 14 benchmark–model pairs, 89% show non-significant Spearman correlation between confidence and calibration gap (p>0.05p>0.05), with permutation tests confirming on MMLU and TruthfulQA (Fig. 1). Theorem 7 is a worst-case bound; the rare significant pairs involve extreme miscalibration (ECE>0.6\mathrm{ECE}>0.6). (2) Phase transition at m⋅ε≈1m\cdot\varepsilon\approx 1 confirmed on all benchmarks. (3) Active querying achieves LL-independent rates on MMLU with slope ratio 1.38–1.48 (theory: 1.50) and L-independence CV =8%=8\% (Fig. 3). (4) Compositional cost grows exponentially in synthetic pipelines (Fig. 4) and a real 2-stage pipeline has L^sys=3.05\hat{L}_{\mathrm{sys}}=3.05 vs. single-model 1.411.41 (2.16×2.16\times; Appendix S). These empirical results align with the practical checklist advertised in the introduction: report the floor, treat below-floor gaps as ties, and switch to active querying when passive resolution saturates.

ECE vs. accuracy floors. The verification tax ((L​ε/n)1/3(L\varepsilon/n)^{1/3}) gives the floor for calibration comparisons; the standard binomial floor (2​ε⁡(1−ε)/n2\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)/n}) gives the floor for accuracy comparisons. On MMLU (n=14,042n{=}14{,}042, ε=0.16\varepsilon{=}0.16, L=1.4L{=}1.4): accuracy floor =0.006=0.006, ECE floor =0.028=0.028—a 4.7×4.7\times gap. Models that are distinguishable on accuracy may still be indistinguishable on calibration. Representative audit tables and the full five-benchmark breakdown are deferred to the appendix.

Extended results across all five benchmarks (14 benchmark–model pairs, ε∈[0.04,1.0]\varepsilon\in[0.04,1.0], verification floors 0.0260.026–0.1390.139) are in Appendix S. Four of five benchmarks have mean verification floors ≥0.05\geq 0.05—above the typical claimed improvement threshold—confirming that only MMLU (n=14,042n{=}14{,}042) is large enough for reliable calibration comparisons.

9 Related Work

Calibration estimation. Sun et al. (2023) and Futami and Fujisawa (2024) established O(n−1/3)O(n^{-1/3}) ECE upper bounds without tracking ε\varepsilon-dependence. We provide the matching lower bound and reveal the phase transition. Hu et al. (2024) study calibration testing (Ω⁡(ε−2.5)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2.5}) complexity); Blasiok et al. (2023) introduce calibration distance.

Active and sequential evaluation. Kossen et al. (2021) propose practical active testing; Theorem 12 provides the matching minimax rate. Shekhar and Ramdas (2024) develop sequential fairness tests; our sequential result (Appendix M) provides the matching lower bound.

Nonparametric functionals. Our lower bound builds on Lepski et al. (1999). The novel observation: the noise variance equals ε\varepsilon, yielding the ε\varepsilon-dependent rate.

10 Conclusion

The verification tax is a law: Θ⁡((L​ε/m)1/3)\Theta((L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}) for passive verification, with no escape via model access, self-evaluation, or strategic miscalibration. Better models are harder to audit; passive benchmarking fails exactly when frontier gaps become small; and active querying is the only route that asymptotically removes the Lipschitz penalty. Practically, papers should report verification floors beside calibration claims, size holdouts via m≥L​ε/δ3m\geq L\varepsilon/\delta^{3}, and treat leaderboard gaps below the floor as ties rather than progress.

Prediction. Under current scaling trends (α≈0.5\alpha\approx 0.5), next-generation frontier models will achieve ε≈0.05\varepsilon\approx 0.05–0.080.08 on MMLU. At this error rate, the verification floor on MMLU (n=14,042n{=}14{,}042) is δfloor≈0.016\delta_{\mathrm{floor}}\approx 0.016–0.0180.018, so we predict that most claimed calibration gains in next-generation technical reports will remain below the detectable floor.

Anonymous software. An anonymized implementation of the verification-floor, holdout-sizing, and verifiability-assessment tools is included in the supplementary material and can be publicly released upon publication.

Limitations and open problems. Our analysis assumes Lipschitz calibration, leaves a logarithmic gap between Theorems 2 and 3, uses worst-case Lipschitz accumulation in composition, and focuses on ECE rather than alternative calibration functionals. Closing the log gap and handling discontinuous or multiclass settings remain open.

Appendix A Full Proof of Theorem 7 and Corollaries

Theorem 7 (Self-Verification Impossibility). Fix any model with weights θ\theta. The outputs (p⁡(xi),z⁡(xi))(p(x_{i}),z(x_{i})) are deterministic functions of xix_{i} and θ\theta; they do not depend on Δ\Delta. Construct: Δ0​(p)=0\Delta_{0}(p)=0 for all pp (ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0); Δ1​(p)=min⁡(L,1)\Delta_{1}(p)=\min(L,1) near 1−ε1-\varepsilon (ECE=min⁡(L,1)\mathrm{ECE}=\min(L,1)). Both are constant and hence in ℱ⁡(L)\mathcal{F}(L). Both produce identical observations. Any label-free estimator VV returns the same value under both: 𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δ0)|]+𝔼⁡[|V−ECE⁡(Δ1)|]≥|ECE⁡(Δ0)−ECE⁡(Δ1)|=min⁡(L,1)\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{0})|]+\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{1})|]\geq|\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{0})-\mathrm{ECE}(\Delta_{1})|=\min(L,1). Taking sup\sup: supΔ𝔼⁡[|V−ECE|]≥min⁡(L,1)/2\sup_{\Delta}\mathbb{E}[|V-\mathrm{ECE}|]\geq\min(L,1)/2. □\square

Corollary 8 (LLM-as-Judge). Judge JJ observes only (xi,fS​(xi))(x_{i},f_{S}(x_{i}))—the same label-free observation space. The two worlds (Δ0\Delta_{0}, Δ1\Delta_{1}) produce identical inputs and outputs for SS, hence identical observations for JJ. The bound follows directly.

Corollary 9 (Hallucination Detection). Factual accuracy: Pr⁡[fact correct∣confidence ​p]=η⁡(p)\Pr[\text{fact correct}\mid\text{confidence }p]=\eta(p). Calibration gap Δ⁡(p)=η⁡(p)−p\Delta(p)=\eta(p)-p. Self-consistency generates kk responses from (x,θ)(x,\theta)—all deterministic functions of the model, independent of Δ\Delta. The bound applies.

Corollary (Pseudo-Label Circularity). Self-labeling with y^i=arg⁡max⁡f⁡(xi)\hat{y}_{i}=\arg\max f(x_{i}) yields ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0 for any deterministic classifier.

Corollary (Distribution Shift). A calibration monitor trained on DtrainD_{\mathrm{train}} cannot detect miscalibration on DtestD_{\mathrm{test}} without labeled samples from DtestD_{\mathrm{test}}.

Appendix B Self-Contained Lower Bound via Bernoulli Two-Prior Method

We prove Theorem 2 directly in the Bernoulli observation model, without invoking asymptotic equivalence to Gaussian white noise.

Setup. We observe mm i.i.d. pairs (pi,Yi)(p_{i},Y_{i}) where pi∼μp_{i}\sim\mu and Yi|pi∼Bern⁡(pi+Δ⁡(pi))Y_{i}\mid p_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p_{i}+\Delta(p_{i})), with Δ∈ℱ⁡(L)\Delta\in\mathcal{F}(L).

Step 1: Parametric submodel. Assume μ\mu has density ≥cμ>0\geq c_{\mu}>0 on a window W=[1−ε−w/2, 1−ε+w/2]W=[1{-}\varepsilon{-}w/2,\,1{-}\varepsilon{+}w/2]. Partition WW into NN subintervals I1,…,INI_{1},\ldots,I_{N} of width h=w/Nh=w/N. Let g:ℝ→[0,1]g:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] be a smooth bump supported on [0,1][0,1] with ∫g=1\int g=1, ‖g‖22=κg\|g\|_{2}^{2}=\kappa_{g}, and Lipschitz constant 1. For θ∈[−1,1]N\theta\in[-1,1]^{N}, define: Δθ​(p)=L​h​∑j=1Nθj​g​((p−tj+h/2)/h)\Delta_{\theta}(p)=Lh\sum_{j=1}^{N}\theta_{j}\,g((p-t_{j}+h/2)/h), where tjt_{j} are the interval midpoints. Each bump has height L​hLh, width hh, and Lipschitz constant LL. Disjoint supports ensure Δθ∈ℱ⁡(L)\Delta_{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}(L).

Step 2: Sufficient statistics. In interval IjI_{j}, there are nj≈m​cμ​hn_{j}\approx mc_{\mu}h observations. The per-bin calibration gap estimate Zj=nj−1∑i:pi∈Ij(Yi−pi)Z_{j}=n_{j}^{-1}\sum_{i:p_{i}\in I_{j}}(Y_{i}-p_{i}) satisfies 𝔼⁡[Zj]≈L​h​θj​g¯j\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}]\approx Lh\theta_{j}\bar{g}_{j} and Var⁡(Zj)≈ε/(m​cμ​h)\mathrm{Var}(Z_{j})\approx\varepsilon/(mc_{\mu}h). Setting α=L​h​g¯j\alpha=Lh\bar{g}_{j} and σ2=ε/(m​cμ​h)\sigma^{2}=\varepsilon/(mc_{\mu}h), the problem reduces to the sequence model Zj≈α​θj+σ​ξjZ_{j}\approx\alpha\theta_{j}+\sigma\xi_{j} with approximately independent ξj\xi_{j}.

Step 3: ECE as L1L_{1} functional. The ECE restricted to WW is ECEW≈cμ​w⋅α⋅F1​(θ)\mathrm{ECE}_{W}\approx c_{\mu}w\cdot\alpha\cdot F_{1}(\theta) where F1​(θ)=N−1​∑j=1N|θj|F_{1}(\theta)=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|\theta_{j}|. Lower-bounding F1F_{1} estimation suffices.

Step 4: Two-prior construction (following Lepski et al., 1999, §4.3). Construct product priors π0=ν0⊗N\pi_{0}=\nu_{0}^{\otimes N}, π1=ν1⊗N\pi_{1}=\nu_{1}^{\otimes N} on [−1,1]N[-1,1]^{N} where ν1−ν0=η​μ\nu_{1}-\nu_{0}=\eta\mu for a signed measure μ\mu with ∫μ=0\int\mu=0 and ∫|t|​μ​(𝑑t)=2​δ\int|t|\mu(dt)=2\delta (the separation in L1L_{1} norm). Both νj\nu_{j} are perturbations of Uniform⁡([−1,1])\mathrm{Uniform}([-1,1]) with density 1/21/2. The per-coordinate KL is KL(pν1∥pν0)≤4α2η2/σ2\mathrm{KL}(p_{\nu_{1}}\|p_{\nu_{0}})\leq 4\alpha^{2}\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}.

Step 5: Bayesian Le Cam bound. Total KL: KLtotal=4​N​α2​η2/σ2\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{total}}=4N\alpha^{2}\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}. Setting KLtotal=1\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{total}}=1: η=σ/(2​α​N)\eta=\sigma/(2\alpha\sqrt{N}). The Bayesian Le Cam bound gives: R∗≥c⋅δη−N−1/2=cδσ/(2αN)−N−1/2R^{*}\geq c\cdot\delta\eta-N^{-1/2}=c\delta\sigma/(2\alpha\sqrt{N})-N^{-1/2}.

Step 6: Optimization over NN. Substituting σ/α=ε​N/(L​w3/2​g¯​m​cμ)\sigma/\alpha=\sqrt{\varepsilon N}/(Lw^{3/2}\bar{g}\sqrt{mc_{\mu}}) and optimizing over NN yields N∗=Θ⁡((m/ε)1/3)N^{*}=\Theta((m/\varepsilon)^{1/3}) and:

RECE∗≥c′​(L​εm)1/3/(log⁡m)c′′R^{*}_{\mathrm{ECE}}\geq c^{\prime}\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{m}\right)^{1/3}/(\log m)^{c^{\prime\prime}}

Appendix C Full Proof of Theorem 12 (Active Verification)

Lower bound. The Le Cam lower bound from Theorem 1 applies unchanged to adaptive strategies. Construct the same two hypotheses: P0P_{0} (calibrated, ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0) and P1P_{1} (miscalibrated by δ\delta near p=1−εp=1-\varepsilon, ECE=δ\mathrm{ECE}=\delta). Under adaptive querying, the auditor selects pip_{i} based on all previous observations (p1,y1,…,pi−1,yi−1)(p_{1},y_{1},\ldots,p_{i-1},y_{i-1}). By the chain rule of KL divergence:

KL(P0m∥P1m)=∑i=1m𝔼[KL(P0(⋅∣pi)∥P1(⋅∣pi))]\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}^{m}\|P_{1}^{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}(\cdot\mid p_{i})\|P_{1}(\cdot\mid p_{i}))\right] (1)

Each term is at most δ2/ε\delta^{2}/\varepsilon (the per-observation KL when pip_{i} is in the miscalibrated region, zero otherwise). Adaptivity does not increase the per-observation information: conditioned on pip_{i}, the label yiy_{i} is a single Bernoulli draw whose KL is δ2/ε\delta^{2}/\varepsilon regardless of previous observations. Therefore KL≤m​δ2/ε\mathrm{KL}\leq m\delta^{2}/\varepsilon, and Le Cam gives Ractive∗≥c​ε/mR^{*}_{\mathrm{active}}\geq c\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}.

Upper bound. We construct a two-phase adaptive strategy.

Phase 1 (Exploration): Select NN equally-spaced confidence levels {pj=j/N}j=1N\{p_{j}=j/N\}_{j=1}^{N} in the interval [1−ε−w,1−ε+w][1-\varepsilon-w,1-\varepsilon+w] for a window width w=O⁡(1)w=O(1). Query each level m/(2​N)m/(2N) times. The empirical estimate Δ^​(pj)\hat{\Delta}(p_{j}) has standard error σj=2​ε​N/m\sigma_{j}=\sqrt{2\varepsilon N/m}. Classify each bin as:

  • •

    Resolved: |Δ^​(pj)|>2​σj|\hat{\Delta}(p_{j})|>2\sigma_{j} — the sign of Δ⁡(pj)\Delta(p_{j}) is known with high probability.

  • •

    Unresolved: |Δ^​(pj)|≤2​σj|\hat{\Delta}(p_{j})|\leq 2\sigma_{j} — the sign is uncertain.

The unresolved zone has width at most 4​σj/L=O⁡(ε​N/m/L)4\sigma_{j}/L=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon N/m}/L) by the Lipschitz constraint (the function can only stay near zero for a region of width ≤|Δ|max/L\leq|\Delta|_{\max}/L).

Phase 2 (Exploitation): Use the remaining m/2m/2 queries on resolved bins to estimate |Δ⁡(pj)|=Δ⁡(pj)⋅sign⁡(Δ⁡(pj))|\Delta(p_{j})|=\Delta(p_{j})\cdot\mathrm{sign}(\Delta(p_{j})) (sign is known, so no absolute value problem). This is a simple average with error ε/m\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}.

Total error:

  • •

    Resolved bins: estimation error O⁡(ε/m)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}).

  • •

    Unresolved bins: the contribution to ECE is at most (max ​|Δ|​ in zone)×(width of zone)(\text{max }|\Delta|\text{ in zone})\times(\text{width of zone}). Since |Δ|≤2​σj|\Delta|\leq 2\sigma_{j} in the zone and the width is O⁡(σj/L)O(\sigma_{j}/L), this contributes O⁡(σj2/L)=O⁡(ε​N/(m​L))O(\sigma_{j}^{2}/L)=O(\varepsilon N/(mL)).

Choose N=L​m/εN=L\sqrt{m/\varepsilon} to balance the two terms. Both become O⁡(ε/m)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}). □\square

Appendix D Regulatory Infeasibility: Full Derivation

From Theorem 3, verification to accuracy δ\delta requires m≥L​ε/δ3m\geq L\varepsilon/\delta^{3}. For KK demographic groups with minimum proportion πmin\pi_{\min}, the effective sample size per group is m​πminm\pi_{\min}. Each group requires L​ε/(πmin​δ3)L\varepsilon/(\pi_{\min}\delta^{3}) total samples. Summing: mtotal≥K⋅L​επmin​δ3m_{\mathrm{total}}\geq K\cdot\frac{L\varepsilon}{\pi_{\min}\delta^{3}}.

EU AI Act Annex III (K=10K{=}10, πmin=0.05\pi_{\min}{=}0.05, δ=0.02\delta{=}0.02, ε=0.05\varepsilon{=}0.05, L=1L{=}1): m≥10⋅1⋅0.05/(0.05⋅0.000008)=1,250,000m\geq 10\cdot 1\cdot 0.05/(0.05\cdot 0.000008)=1{,}250{,}000. Available: ∼\sim707K (CheXpert + MIMIC-CXR + NIH ChestXray14). Gap: 1.8×1.8\times.

FDA SaMD (K=8K{=}8, πmin=0.05\pi_{\min}{=}0.05, δ=0.01\delta{=}0.01, ε=0.02\varepsilon{=}0.02): m≥3,200,000m\geq 3{,}200{,}000. Gap: 4.5×4.5\times.

Under active verification, the requirement drops to K​ε/(πmin​δ2)K\varepsilon/(\pi_{\min}\delta^{2}), making all three frameworks feasible—but requiring infrastructure that does not yet exist.

Appendix E Extended Benchmark Analysis

Leaderboard noise. Across 57 MMLU subjects, we compute pairwise accuracy gaps between 3 models and compare to per-subject verification floors. Results: 37/57 subjects (65%) are completely unranked; 56/57 (98%) have at least one unranked pair; 132/171 pairwise comparisons (77%) fall below the floor. Mean ranking instability under 80%-bootstrap: 29.1%.

Appendix F Extended Empirical Results

Five-benchmark validation. We validate across MMLU (14,042), TruthfulQA (817), ARC-Challenge (1,172), HellaSwag (10,042), and WinoGrande (1,267) with 3 models, yielding 14 valid benchmark–model pairs. Figure 6 shows verification floors per benchmark; Figures 7–9 show detailed TruthfulQA analysis.

Real 2-stage pipeline. A pipeline of Llama-3.1-405B (stage 1) and Qwen3-Next-80B (stage 2) on MMLU yields L^sys=3.05\hat{L}_{\mathrm{sys}}=3.05 vs. single-model L^=1.41\hat{L}=1.41 (2.16×2.16\times), confirming that composed systems have higher Lipschitz constants and correspondingly higher verification floors (Figures 10–11).

Permutation tests. For the self-evaluation claim (Theorem 7), we supplement Spearman correlations with 10,000-permutation tests under H0H_{0}: confidence is independent of calibration gap. Results: MMLU 2/3 models p>0.10p>0.10 (non-significant); TruthfulQA 2/3 models p>0.10p>0.10. The positive control (confidence vs. accuracy) is significant on both benchmarks (p<0.001p<0.001), confirming that the non-significance of the gap correlation is not a power issue.

Bootstrap methodology. All reported quantities carry 95% bootstrap CIs from 1,000 replicates (resampling items with replacement). Lipschitz estimates have wide CIs (e.g., Llama-405B: L^=1.41\hat{L}=1.41 [1.13, 3.02]) because finite-difference estimation is inherently noisy; ECE and ε\varepsilon CIs are tight (e.g., ECE=0.118\mathrm{ECE}=0.118 [0.113, 0.124]).

Appendix H Full Proof of Theorem 1 (Le Cam Lower Bound)

Construct two hypotheses. Fix a classifier whose score distribution places all mass at p0=1−εp_{0}=1-\varepsilon.

  • •

    P0P_{0}: Y|p⁡(X)=p0∼Bern⁡(1−ε)Y\mid p(X)=p_{0}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1-\varepsilon). Calibrated: η⁡(p0)=p0\eta(p_{0})=p_{0}, so ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0.

  • •

    P1P_{1}: Y|p⁡(X)=p0∼Bern⁡(1−ε−δ)Y\mid p(X)=p_{0}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1-\varepsilon-\delta). Miscalibrated: ECE=δ\mathrm{ECE}=\delta.

Both hypotheses use a constant calibration gap (Lipschitz constant 0), so Δ∈ℱ⁡(L)\Delta\in\mathcal{F}(L) for all L>0L>0. The KL divergence of mm i.i.d. samples is:

KL(P0m∥P1m)=m⋅KL(Bern(1−ε)∥Bern(1−ε−δ))=m​δ2ε⁡(1−ε)≤m​δ2ε\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}^{m}\|P_{1}^{m})=m\cdot\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Bern}(1-\varepsilon)\|\mathrm{Bern}(1-\varepsilon-\delta))=\frac{m\delta^{2}}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}\leq\frac{m\delta^{2}}{\varepsilon}

where the last inequality uses 1−ε≤11-\varepsilon\leq 1 and the KL approximation KL(Bern(p)∥Bern(p+δ))≈δ2/(p(1−p))\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\|\mathrm{Bern}(p+\delta))\approx\delta^{2}/(p(1-p)) (valid for δ≤ε/2\delta\leq\varepsilon/2). By Le Cam’s lemma [Tsybakov, 2009]:

R∗≥δ2(1−TV(P0m,P1m))≥δ2e−KL(P0m∥P1m)R^{*}\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\left(1-\mathrm{TV}(P_{0}^{m},P_{1}^{m})\right)\geq\frac{\delta}{2}e^{-\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}^{m}\|P_{1}^{m})}

where the second inequality uses Bretagnolle–Huber. Setting KL=1\mathrm{KL}=1 (i.e., δ=ε/m\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}): R∗≥(1/2​e)​ε/m≈0.184​ε/mR^{*}\geq(1/2e)\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}\approx 0.184\sqrt{\varepsilon/m}. □\square

H.1 Direct Bernoulli Lower Bound (Alternative to Brown–Low)

For readers who prefer a self-contained argument avoiding asymptotic equivalence, we sketch a direct Assouad-type lower bound in the Bernoulli model.

Partition [0,1][0,1] into BB equal-width bins. Consider the class of calibration functions Δω​(p)=h⋅ωb\Delta_{\omega}(p)=h\cdot\omega_{b} for p∈Ibp\in I_{b}, where ω=(ω1,…,ωB)∈{−1,+1}B\omega=(\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{B})\in\{-1,+1\}^{B} and h>0h>0 is chosen so that Δω\Delta_{\omega} is LL-Lipschitz (requiring h≤L/(2​B)h\leq L/(2B)). Each Δω\Delta_{\omega} has ECE=h\mathrm{ECE}=h (since ∑b(1/B)​|h⋅ωb|=h\sum_{b}(1/B)|h\cdot\omega_{b}|=h). For any two configurations ω,ω′\omega,\omega^{\prime} differing in one coordinate bb, the KL divergence of the m/Bm/B observations in bin bb is:

KL=mB⋅(2​h)2ε⁡(1−ε)≤4​m​h2B​ε\mathrm{KL}=\frac{m}{B}\cdot\frac{(2h)^{2}}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}\leq\frac{4mh^{2}}{B\varepsilon}

By Assouad’s lemma [Tsybakov, 2009], the minimax risk satisfies:

R∗≥B​h2​(1−2​m​h2B​ε)R^{*}\geq\frac{Bh}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{2mh^{2}}{B\varepsilon}}\right)

Setting h=c​B​ε/mh=c\sqrt{B\varepsilon/m} for a small constant cc and B=⌊(L​m/ε)1/3⌋B=\lfloor(Lm/\varepsilon)^{1/3}\rfloor gives:

R∗≥c′​(L​εm)1/3R^{*}\geq c^{\prime}\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{m}\right)^{1/3}

This recovers the (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3} rate directly from the Bernoulli model, confirming the Brown–Low reduction. The constant c′c^{\prime} is weaker than the one obtained via Lepski et al. [1999], but the argument is fully self-contained. □\square

Appendix I Full Proof of Theorem 3 (Matched Upper Bound)

Bias-variance decomposition. With BB equal-width bins and mm total samples:

1. Bias. Within each bin of width 1/B1/B, the calibration gap Δ\Delta varies by at most L/BL/B (Lipschitz). By the Bridge Lemma, |ECEB−CEsmooth|≤L/B|\mathrm{ECE}_{B}-\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{smooth}}|\leq L/B.

2. Variance. Each bin bb has nb≈m/Bn_{b}\approx m/B samples. (Under bounded density cμ≤d​μ/d​p≤Cμc_{\mu}\leq d\mu/dp\leq C_{\mu}; equal-mass binning achieves nb=m/Bn_{b}=m/B exactly when μ\mu concentrates.) The empirical calibration gap has variance Var⁡(Δ^b)≤σ2/nb≈σ2​B/m\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\Delta}_{b})\leq\sigma^{2}/n_{b}\approx\sigma^{2}B/m, where σ2=maxb⁡𝔼⁡[η⁡(p)​(1−η⁡(p))∣p∈Ib]\sigma^{2}=\max_{b}\mathbb{E}[\eta(p)(1-\eta(p))\mid p\in I_{b}]. Estimation error: 𝔼⁡[|ECE^B−ECEB|]≤σ2​B/m\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}_{B}-\mathrm{ECE}_{B}|]\leq\sqrt{\sigma^{2}B/m}.

3. Total error. L/B+σ2​B/mL/B+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}B/m}.

4. Optimization. Setting L/B=σ2​B/mL/B=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}B/m}: B∗=(L2​m/σ2)1/3B^{*}=(L^{2}m/\sigma^{2})^{1/3}, total error (L​σ2/m)1/3(L\sigma^{2}/m)^{1/3}. In the rare-error regime σ2≈ε\sigma^{2}\approx\varepsilon, recovering the headline rate. □\square

Appendix J Verification Dynamics, Recalibration Trap, and Half-Life

J.1 Verification Dynamics

Suppose a model is deployed at rate rr samples per unit time and ε⁡(t)=c0​t−β\varepsilon(t)=c_{0}t^{-\beta}. The verification floor at time tt is δfloor(t)=(Lc0/r)1/3t−(β+1)/3\delta_{\mathrm{floor}}(t)=(Lc_{0}/r)^{1/3}t^{-(\beta+1)/3}. Meaningful verification (δfloor​(t)<ε⁡(t)\delta_{\mathrm{floor}}(t)<\varepsilon(t)) reduces to (L/(r​c02))1/3<t(1−2​β)/3(L/(rc_{0}^{2}))^{1/3}<t^{(1-2\beta)/3}. This is satisfied for large tt when β<1/2\beta<1/2, violated when β>1/2\beta>1/2, and equivalent to L/(r​c02)<1L/(rc_{0}^{2})<1 when β=1/2\beta=1/2. Critical exponent: β∗=1/2\beta^{*}=1/2 (passive), βactive∗=1\beta^{*}_{\mathrm{active}}=1 (active). □\square

J.2 Recalibration Trap

With ECEK=γK​ECE0\mathrm{ECE}_{K}=\gamma^{K}\mathrm{ECE}_{0}, the improvement from round KK to K+1K+1 is γK​ECE0​(1−γ)\gamma^{K}\mathrm{ECE}_{0}(1-\gamma). Distinguishing requires (Theorem 1) mK≥ε/(γ2​K​ECE02​(1−γ)2)m_{K}\geq\varepsilon/(\gamma^{2K}\mathrm{ECE}_{0}^{2}(1-\gamma)^{2}). Setting mK=Mtotalm_{K}=M_{\mathrm{total}} gives K∗=⌊log⁡(Mtotal​(1−γ)2​ECE02/ε)/(2​log⁡(1/γ))⌋K^{*}=\lfloor\log(M_{\mathrm{total}}(1-\gamma)^{2}\mathrm{ECE}_{0}^{2}/\varepsilon)/(2\log(1/\gamma))\rfloor.

Worked example (MMLU). γ=0.5\gamma=0.5, ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05, ECE0=0.10\mathrm{ECE}_{0}=0.10, Mtotal=14,000M_{\mathrm{total}}=14{,}000: K∗=⌊6.55/1.386⌋=4K^{*}=\lfloor 6.55/1.386\rfloor=4. After 4 halving rounds, MMLU cannot verify further improvement.

J.3 Verification Half-Life

Let ECE drift rate λ\lambda satisfy |ECE⁡(t)−ECE⁡(0)|≤λ​t|\mathrm{ECE}(t)-\mathrm{ECE}(0)|\leq\lambda t. (i) The verification becomes invalid after t1/2=δ/λt_{1/2}=\delta/\lambda. (ii) Perpetual verification requires data rate r≥L​ε​λ/δ4r\geq L\varepsilon\lambda/\delta^{4}.

Domain estimates (assuming L=1L=1, ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05): Medical AI (λ=0.01\lambda=0.01/month, δ=0.02\delta=0.02): t1/2=2t_{1/2}=2 months, r≈3,100r\approx 3{,}100/month. Content moderation: 6 months, 620/month. Financial trading (λ=0.1\lambda=0.1/week, δ=0.01\delta=0.01): t1/2=17t_{1/2}=17 hours. Autonomous driving: 15 days. Static benchmarks have the same half-life: a benchmark constructed at t=0t=0 decays at rate λ\lambda, formalizing the case for periodic refresh.

Appendix K Alternative Derivation of Theorem 2 via Asymptotic Equivalence

Step 1: Reduction to nonparametric regression.

Within a window of width ww around p=1−εp=1-\varepsilon, where the score distribution concentrates, the calibration verification problem reduces to estimating the L1L_{1} norm of a regression function. Specifically:

For p∈[1−ε−w/2, 1−ε+w/2]p\in[1-\varepsilon-w/2,\,1-\varepsilon+w/2], define Δ⁡(p)=η⁡(p)−p\Delta(p)=\eta(p)-p. The labels YiY_{i} given p⁡(Xi)=pp(X_{i})=p are Bern⁡(η⁡(p))=Bern⁡(p+Δ⁡(p))\mathrm{Bern}(\eta(p))=\mathrm{Bern}(p+\Delta(p)), with variance η⁡(p)​(1−η⁡(p))≈ε\eta(p)(1-\eta(p))\approx\varepsilon in the rare-error regime.

The ECE restricted to this window is:

ECEwindow=∫1−ε−w/21−ε+w/2|Δ⁡(p)|​𝑑μ​(p)\mathrm{ECE}_{\text{window}}=\int_{1-\varepsilon-w/2}^{1-\varepsilon+w/2}|\Delta(p)|\,d\mu(p) (2)

This is precisely the L1L_{1} norm of Δ\Delta on the window, weighted by μ\mu.

Step 2: Identification with L1L_{1} functional estimation in white noise.

By the asymptotic equivalence of nonparametric regression and Gaussian white noise [Brown and Low, 1996, Nussbaum, 1996], estimating ∫|Δ⁡(p)|​𝑑p\int|\Delta(p)|dp from mm observations with per-observation variance ε\varepsilon is asymptotically equivalent to estimating ∫|f⁡(t)|​𝑑t\int|f(t)|dt in the white noise model:

dX(t)=f(t)dt+(m/ε)−1/2dW(t),t∈[0,1]dX(t)=f(t)dt+(m/\varepsilon)^{-1/2}dW(t),\quad t\in[0,1] (3)

with effective sample size neff=m/εn_{\mathrm{eff}}=m/\varepsilon and f∈Σ⁡(β=1,L)f\in\Sigma(\beta=1,L) (Lipschitz = Hölder with β=1\beta=1).

Step 3: Application of Lepski, Nemirovski & Spokoiny (1999).

By Theorem 2.2 of Lepski et al. [1999], the minimax rate for estimating the L1L_{1} norm of a β\beta-Hölder function in white noise with sample size nn is:

RL1∗≥c⋅n−β/(2β+1)/(logn)c′R^{*}_{L_{1}}\geq c\cdot n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}/(\log n)^{c^{\prime}} (4)

For β=1\beta=1 (Lipschitz) and n=neff=m/εn=n_{\mathrm{eff}}=m/\varepsilon:

RL1∗≥c⋅(m/ε)−1/3/(log(m/ε))c′=c⋅(εm)1/3/(logm)c′R^{*}_{L_{1}}\geq c\cdot(m/\varepsilon)^{-1/3}/(\log(m/\varepsilon))^{c^{\prime}}=c\cdot\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{m}\right)^{1/3}/(\log m)^{c^{\prime}} (5)

Incorporating the Lipschitz constant LL (which scales the function class):

R∗​(m,ε,L)≥c2​(L​εm)1/3/(log⁡m)c3R^{*}(m,\varepsilon,L)\geq c_{2}\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{m}\right)^{1/3}/(\log m)^{c_{3}} (6)

Technical conditions:

  • •

    Score-mass concentration: The score distribution μ\mu must place mass ≥ρ\geq\rho in a window of width ww around 1−ε1-\varepsilon. We state this as an assumption. This holds for well-trained classifiers: overconfident models concentrate predictions near the top.

  • •

    The Brown–Low equivalence requires mm sufficiently large relative to the smoothness. The minimum mm is m≥C⁡(L)/εm\geq C(L)/\varepsilon for a constant depending on LL.

  • •

    Lipschitz constant: Since Δ⁡(p)=η⁡(p)−p\Delta(p)=\eta(p)-p and p↦pp\mapsto p is 1-Lipschitz, we have LΔ≤Lη+1L_{\Delta}\leq L_{\eta}+1. We use LL throughout for LΔL_{\Delta}.

Clarification on the asymptotic regime.

The Brown–Low equivalence is applied in the limit m→∞m\to\infty with ε\varepsilon fixed. The error rate ε\varepsilon is a property of the model under audit, not an asymptotic parameter. For any fixed ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2), the Bernoulli label variance ε⁡(1−ε)≥ε/2>0\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\geq\varepsilon/2>0 is bounded away from zero, satisfying the regularity conditions. The ε\varepsilon-dependence in the rate (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3} arises from substituting σ2=ε⁡(1−ε)≈ε\sigma^{2}=\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\approx\varepsilon into the white-noise minimax rate with neff=m/εn_{\mathrm{eff}}=m/\varepsilon, not from taking ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 within the equivalence framework.

Appendix L Supplementary Details for Theorem 11

The proof of Theorem 11 in the main text is complete. We note that the result extends straightforwardly to any side information 𝒮\mathcal{S} that is independent of the fresh evaluation labels conditional on the scores. This includes: model weights, architecture specifications, training data, training logs, gradient histories, and any derived quantity (e.g., Fisher information matrices, Hessian spectra, pruning masks). The key insight is that calibration is a property of the model-world interface, not of the model alone.

Appendix M Full Proof of Sequential Verification

Lower bound. Under the two Le Cam hypotheses (P0P_{0}: ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0, P1P_{1}: ECE=δ\mathrm{ECE}=\delta), the log-likelihood ratio after tt observations is:

Λt=∑i=1tlog⁡p1​(yi∣pi)p0​(yi∣pi)\Lambda_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\log\frac{p_{1}(y_{i}\mid p_{i})}{p_{0}(y_{i}\mid p_{i})} (7)

This is a random walk with per-step drift:

𝔼P0[Λ1]=−KL(P0(⋅∣pi)∥P1(⋅∣pi))≈−δ2ε\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[\Lambda_{1}]=-\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}(\cdot\mid p_{i})\|P_{1}(\cdot\mid p_{i}))\approx-\frac{\delta^{2}}{\varepsilon} (8)

By Wald’s identity for sequential testing [Tsybakov, 2009], any test between P0P_{0} and P1P_{1} with error probabilities ≤α\leq\alpha satisfies:

𝔼⁡[τ]≥log⁡(1/α)KL(P0∥P1)=ε​log⁡(1/α)δ2\mathbb{E}[\tau]\geq\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}{\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{1})}=\frac{\varepsilon\log(1/\alpha)}{\delta^{2}} (9)

Since any sequential verification protocol with accuracy δ\delta at confidence 1−α1-\alpha must distinguish ECE=0\mathrm{ECE}=0 from ECE=δ\mathrm{ECE}=\delta with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha, the lower bound follows.

Upper bound. We construct a confidence sequence for the ECE using the method of mixtures [Howard et al., 2021]. Define the running ECE estimate:

ECE^t=∑b=1Bnb,tt​|Δ^b,t|\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}_{t}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{n_{b,t}}{t}\left|\hat{\Delta}_{b,t}\right| (10)

where Δ^b,t\hat{\Delta}_{b,t} is the empirical calibration gap in bin bb after tt observations.

By Theorem 1 of Howard et al. [2021], there exists a time-uniform confidence sequence (Ct)t≥1(C_{t})_{t\geq 1} such that:

Pr(∃t≥1:|ECE^t−ECE|>Ct)≤α\Pr\left(\exists t\geq 1:|\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}_{t}-\mathrm{ECE}|>C_{t}\right)\leq\alpha (11)

with Ct=O⁡(ε​log⁡(log⁡(t)/α)/t)C_{t}=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon\log(\log(t)/\alpha)/t}).

Define the stopping time τ=inf{t:Ct≤δ}\tau=\inf\{t:C_{t}\leq\delta\}. Solving Ct≤δC_{t}\leq\delta:

ε​log⁡(log⁡(t)/α)t≤δ⟹t≥ε​log⁡(log⁡(t)/α)δ2\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon\log(\log(t)/\alpha)}{t}}\leq\delta\implies t\geq\frac{\varepsilon\log(\log(t)/\alpha)}{\delta^{2}} (12)

For the dominant term, 𝔼⁡[τ]=O⁡(ε​log⁡(1/α)/δ2)\mathbb{E}[\tau]=O(\varepsilon\log(1/\alpha)/\delta^{2}), matching the lower bound up to constants. □\square

Appendix N Temperature Scaling Analysis

We provide the full proof of the temperature scaling rate proposition.

Step 1: MLE for the temperature parameter. Given scores p1,…,pmp_{1},\ldots,p_{m} and labels y1,…,ymy_{1},\ldots,y_{m}, the negative log-likelihood is:

ℓ(T)=−∑i=1m[yilogσ(logit(pi)/T)+(1−yi)log(1−σ(logit(pi)/T))]\ell(T)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[y_{i}\log\sigma(\mathrm{logit}(p_{i})/T)+(1-y_{i})\log(1-\sigma(\mathrm{logit}(p_{i})/T))\right] (13)

This is a 1D convex optimization. The MLE T^\hat{T} is unique.

Step 2: Asymptotic normality of MLE. By standard M-estimation theory [van der Vaart, 1998]:

m​(T^−T∗)→𝑑N⁡(0,ℐ​(T∗)−1)\sqrt{m}(\hat{T}-T^{*})\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\mathcal{I}(T^{*})^{-1}) (14)

where ℐ⁡(T∗)\mathcal{I}(T^{*}) is the Fisher information. At T∗=1T^{*}=1, the score function is:

∂∂Tlogp(Y∣p,T)|T=1=−(Y−p)⋅logit(p)\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\log p(Y\mid p,T)\bigg|_{T=1}=-(Y-p)\cdot\mathrm{logit}(p) (15)

So:

ℐ⁡(1)=𝔼⁡[(Y−p)2⋅logit​(p)2]=𝔼⁡[p⁡(1−p)⋅logit​(p)2]\mathcal{I}(1)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-p)^{2}\cdot\mathrm{logit}(p)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[p(1-p)\cdot\mathrm{logit}(p)^{2}] (16)

In the rare-error regime with scores concentrated near 1−ε1-\varepsilon: logit⁡(1−ε)≈log⁡(1/ε)\mathrm{logit}(1-\varepsilon)\approx\log(1/\varepsilon) and p⁡(1−p)≈εp(1-p)\approx\varepsilon, giving:

ℐ⁡(1)≈ε⋅log2⁡(1/ε)\mathcal{I}(1)\approx\varepsilon\cdot\log^{2}(1/\varepsilon) (17)

This is positive and grows as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 — rare errors make temperature estimation easier because logits are more spread out. The MLE satisfies: |T^−T∗|=Op​(1/m⋅ℐ⁡(T∗))|\hat{T}-T^{*}|=O_{p}(1/\sqrt{m\cdot\mathcal{I}(T^{*})}).

Step 3: Translating to calibration error. By Taylor expansion of Δ⁡(p,T)\Delta(p;T) around T∗=1T^{*}=1:

Δ⁡(p,T^)≈∂Δ∂T|T=1⋅(T^−1)=p⁡(1−p)⋅logit⁡(p)⋅(T^−1)\Delta(p;\hat{T})\approx\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial T}\bigg|_{T=1}\cdot(\hat{T}-1)=p(1-p)\cdot\mathrm{logit}(p)\cdot(\hat{T}-1) (18)

So the smooth CE is:

CEsmooth=∫|Δ⁡(p,T^)|​𝑑μ​(p)≈|T^−1|⋅∫p⁡(1−p)​|logit⁡(p)|​dμ​(p)⏟κ\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{smooth}}=\int|\Delta(p;\hat{T})|\,d\mu(p)\approx|\hat{T}-1|\cdot\underbrace{\int p(1-p)|\mathrm{logit}(p)|\,d\mu(p)}_{\kappa} (19)

where κ\kappa is a constant depending on the score distribution. Substituting |T^−1|=Op​(1/m⋅ℐ⁡(T∗))|\hat{T}-1|=O_{p}(1/\sqrt{m\cdot\mathcal{I}(T^{*})}):

CEsmooth=Op​(κm⋅ℐ⁡(T∗))=Op​(1m)\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{smooth}}=O_{p}\left(\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{m\cdot\mathcal{I}(T^{*})}}\right)=O_{p}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right) (20)

with a constant that depends on ε\varepsilon through ℐ⁡(T∗)\mathcal{I}(T^{*}) and κ\kappa. This is the parametric rate m−1/2m^{-1/2}, not the nonparametric rate (L​ε/m)1/3(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}.

Step 4: Connection to binned ECE. Via the Bridge Lemma: ECEB≤CEsmooth+L/B\mathrm{ECE}_{B}\leq\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{smooth}}+L/B. Taking B=O⁡(m/L)B=O(\sqrt{m}/L):

ECEB=O⁡(1/m)\mathrm{ECE}_{B}=O(1/\sqrt{m}) (21)

Comparison to nonparametric rate: The ratio is (1/m)/(Lε/m)1/3=(Lε)−1/3/m1/6(1/\sqrt{m})/(L\varepsilon/m)^{1/3}=(L\varepsilon)^{-1/3}/m^{1/6}, which shrinks with mm. For m=10,000m=10{,}000 and L​ε=0.05L\varepsilon=0.05: ratio ≈0.05\approx 0.05. Temperature scaling is ∼\sim20×\times more data-efficient than nonparametric ECE estimation. □\square

Appendix O Verification Transfer Details

We provide the full proof of the verification transfer proposition.

Step 1: Problem reduction. Since Δ1​(p)\Delta_{1}(p) is known (from prior verification), estimating ECE⁡(M2)=∫|Δ2​(p)|​𝑑μ​(p)\mathrm{ECE}(M_{2})=\int|\Delta_{2}(p)|\,d\mu(p) reduces to estimating the shift h⁡(p)=Δ2​(p)−Δ1​(p)h(p)=\Delta_{2}(p)-\Delta_{1}(p), then computing ∫|Δ1​(p)+h^​(p)|​𝑑μ​(p)\int|\Delta_{1}(p)+\hat{h}(p)|\,d\mu(p).

Step 2: Lower bound (detection cost). Two-sample Le Cam between H0H_{0}: Δ2=Δ1\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{1} and H1H_{1}: Δ2=Δ1+h\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{1}+h with ‖h‖∞=δft\|h\|_{\infty}=\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}. From m2m_{2} fresh samples near p≈1−ε2p\approx 1-\varepsilon_{2}:

KL(H0m2∥H1m2)≈m2​δft2ε2\mathrm{KL}(H_{0}^{m_{2}}\|H_{1}^{m_{2}})\approx\frac{m_{2}\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}^{2}}{\varepsilon_{2}} (22)

Indistinguishable when KL≤1\mathrm{KL}\leq 1, requiring m2=Ω⁡(ε2/δft2)m_{2}=\Omega(\varepsilon_{2}/\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}^{2}).

Step 3: Upper bound (estimation with transfer). Apply Theorem 3 to hh instead of Δ2\Delta_{2}. The histogram estimator for hh has bias Lh/BL_{h}/B and variance ε2​B/m2\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2}B/m_{2}}. Optimizing: B∗=(Lh2​m2/ε2)1/3B^{*}=(L_{h}^{2}m_{2}/\varepsilon_{2})^{1/3}, giving:

‖h^−h‖=O⁡((Lh​ε2m2)1/3)\|\hat{h}-h\|=O\left(\left(\frac{L_{h}\varepsilon_{2}}{m_{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right) (23)

By the triangle inequality:

|ECE⁡(M2)−ECE^​(M2)|≤∫|h^​(p)−h⁡(p)|​𝑑μ​(p)=O⁡((Lh​ε2m2)1/3)\left|\mathrm{ECE}(M_{2})-\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}(M_{2})\right|\leq\int|\hat{h}(p)-h(p)|\,d\mu(p)=O\left(\left(\frac{L_{h}\varepsilon_{2}}{m_{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right) (24)

Setting this equal to δft\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}: m2=O⁡(Lh​ε2/δft3)m_{2}=O(L_{h}\varepsilon_{2}/\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}^{3}).

Step 4: When does transfer help? From-scratch: m2=Θ⁡(L​ε2/δ3)m_{2}=\Theta(L\varepsilon_{2}/\delta^{3}). With transfer: m2=Θ⁡(Lh​ε2/δft3)m_{2}=\Theta(L_{h}\varepsilon_{2}/\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}^{3}). Transfer helps when δft<δ\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}<\delta and Lh≤LL_{h}\leq L. With δft=δ/10\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}=\delta/10, saving is 1000×1000\times. Transfer provides no benefit when δft≥δ\delta_{\mathrm{ft}}\geq\delta. □\square

Appendix P Corrections: Correlation, Heterogeneity, Pre-Calibration

The core theorems assume i.i.d. labeled samples with independent Bernoulli noise. In practice, several deviations may arise.

Temporal correlation.

If evaluation samples arrive sequentially and exhibit temporal dependence, the effective sample size is reduced by a factor depending on the mixing time. For β\beta-mixing sequences with coefficient β⁡(k)≤c⋅ρk\beta(k)\leq c\cdot\rho^{k}, the effective sample size is meff≈m⋅(1−ρ)m_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx m\cdot(1-\rho). All bounds apply with mm replaced by meffm_{\mathrm{eff}}.

Domain heterogeneity.

When the evaluation set spans multiple domains with different error rates, the per-domain verification floor (Fix 3) accounts for this heterogeneity. The overall ECE is a weighted average of domain-specific ECEs, and Jensen’s inequality ensures the overall verification floor is no larger than the worst per-domain floor weighted by domain proportion.

Pre-calibration via RLHF.

Models that have undergone reinforcement learning from human feedback may have artificially smooth calibration functions (small LL), which reduces the verification tax. However, if the RLHF procedure oversmooths, the remaining miscalibration may be concentrated at specific confidence levels, violating the uniform Lipschitz assumption. Domain-specific Lipschitz estimates should be used in such cases.

Appendix Q Numerical Sanity Checks

Q.1 Sharp Le Cam Constants

For each ε\varepsilon, we numerically optimize the Le Cam lower bound over the separation parameter δ\delta, using the exact Bernoulli KL divergence (not the quadratic approximation). We compute three versions: the Bretagnolle–Huber bound R∗≥(δ/2)​exp⁡(−KL)R^{*}\geq(\delta/2)\exp(-\mathrm{KL}), the Pinsker bound R∗≥(δ/2)​(1−KL/2)R^{*}\geq(\delta/2)(1-\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}/2}), and the exact bound via the Bernoulli likelihood ratio test. Table 8 reports the tightest constant for each ε\varepsilon.

The constant c1​(ε)c_{1}(\varepsilon) is monotonically decreasing in ε\varepsilon: smaller error rates yield tighter constants because the Bernoulli variance is smaller and the KL approximation is sharper. All values fall in [0.28,0.38][0.28,0.38], consistent with the theoretical prediction c1≥1/(2​e)≈0.184c_{1}\geq 1/(2e)\approx 0.184 from the quadratic KL approximation. The exact constants are roughly 2×2\times larger, reflecting the tightness gained from exact Bernoulli KL computation.

Appendix S Real-Model Experiment Details

MMLU experimental protocol.

We query each NIM-hosted model with the standard 4-way multiple-choice prompt (“Answer the following multiple choice question. Reply with ONLY the letter (A, B, C, or D)”). For each question, we extract the logprobs of the four answer tokens A, B, C, D at the first generated position, apply softmax over those four logits, and take the maximum as the model’s confidence. The model’s predicted answer is the argmax. Records with API errors (e.g., 403 Forbidden, content-filter rejection) are excluded. Each model run uses a single deterministic temperature-0 generation per question.

Confidence saturation (full data, N=14,042N=14{,}042 each).

On the complete MMLU set, max-softmax confidence is heavily concentrated near 1: Llama-3.1-405B has mean confidence 0.96 with 77% of questions saturated (>0.99>0.99); Qwen3-Next-80B has mean 0.98 with 86% saturated; Llama-4-Maverick-17B has mean 0.99 with 92% saturated. The 405B model has the most spread (lowest saturation rate), as expected for a larger and more capable model. Saturation affects the resolution of high-confidence bins but not the convergence rate, which is governed by the optimal bin count B∗B^{*}.

Lipschitz constant estimation.

For each model, we partition the score range into 20 equal-width bins, compute the empirical accuracy in each bin with at least 30 samples, take the calibration gap Δ^b=accb−pb\hat{\Delta}_{b}=\mathrm{acc}_{b}-p_{b} at each bin center, and form the adjacent-bin slope |Δ^b+1−Δ^b|/|pb+1−pb||\hat{\Delta}_{b+1}-\hat{\Delta}_{b}|/|p_{b+1}-p_{b}|. We report the 75th percentile of these slopes, capped at L^=5\hat{L}=5, as a robust estimate. This is sensitive to bin choice and noise; we recommend the audit floor be reported with L^\hat{L} from at least two binning resolutions.

Pseudo-classifier control experiment.

As a sanity check before running the real-model experiment, we constructed a 10-class softmax classifier from Gaussian logits with ε≈0.10\varepsilon\approx 0.10 (N=20,000N=20{,}000, full-dataset ECE ≈0.31\approx 0.31). Subsampling at m∈{50,…,104}m\in\{50,\ldots,10^{4}\} with optimal B∗B^{*} bins (200 replicates per mm) confirms that (i) the verification floor (red dashed in Figure 14) tracks the empirical std of estimates across the full range, and (ii) the phase transition near m⋅ε≈1m\cdot\varepsilon\approx 1 is visible (Figure 15). The pseudo-classifier results match the MMLU real-model findings of Section 8.

Appendix T Full Proof of Theorem 13 (Compositional Verification)

Lipschitz composition. By the chain rule, if gkg_{k} is LkL_{k}-Lipschitz in its first argument, then gK∘⋯∘g1g_{K}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1} is (∏k=1KLk)(\prod_{k=1}^{K}L_{k})-Lipschitz. Since Δsys​(p)=ηsys​(p)−p\Delta_{\mathrm{sys}}(p)=\eta_{\mathrm{sys}}(p)-p and p↦pp\mapsto p is 1-Lipschitz, Lsys≤∏kLk+1L_{\mathrm{sys}}\leq\prod_{k}L_{k}+1.

Verification cost. Applying Theorem 3 with L=LsysL=L_{\mathrm{sys}}: msys=Θ⁡(Lsys​ε/δ3)m_{\mathrm{sys}}=\Theta(L_{\mathrm{sys}}\varepsilon/\delta^{3}). For homogeneous Lk=LL_{k}=L: Lsys≈LKL_{\mathrm{sys}}\approx L^{K}, giving exponential scaling. □\square

Agent loop bound. For an agent with KK reasoning iterations and L=2L=2: L10=1024L^{10}=1024, L20>106L^{20}>10^{6}.

Caveats. The Lipschitz composition model is optimistic in two directions: discontinuous components (e.g., discrete retrieval) yield Lk=∞L_{k}=\infty, making end-to-end verification impossible at any sample size; conversely, contractive components (Lk<1L_{k}<1) reduce the effective LsysL_{\mathrm{sys}}. Empirical estimation of LsysL_{\mathrm{sys}} via finite-difference approximation is recommended before applying the exponential bound. Independence of per-component calibration gaps is also assumed; correlated miscalibration can either help or hurt depending on structure.

Worked example. A two-stage retriever–classifier with L=2L=2 each gives Lsys≤5L_{\mathrm{sys}}\leq 5, requiring 5×5\times the data of a single classifier. With L=3L=3: 10×10\times. A three-stage pipeline at L=2L=2: 9×9\times; at L=3L=3: 28×28\times.
